overview: Celtic kingdoms is a shifting medieval map label, not one empire. In 800 and 900 the outline covers Strathclyde and Cumbria; from 1000 it switches to Ireland, Wales and a small Kintyre area. These regions had different rulers and histories. The broad outlines conceal rival kingdoms, Norse-linked towns and later English-controlled lands; the dates 800-1279 describe map coverage.

periods.title: The map begins among the Clyde Britons
periods.summary: Dumbarton and then probably Govan anchored a British kingdom; the siege of 870 reshaped its political geography.

periods.title: Irish and Welsh regional powers
periods.summary: The map shifts west and south. Brian Boru’s high-kingship and the Clontarf conflict illustrate Ireland’s competing rulers.

periods.title: Conquest and continuing princely courts
periods.summary: Anglo-Norman expansion transformed Ireland, while Welsh rulers maintained courts such as thirteenth-century Llys Rhosyr.

sections.title: Strathclyde: a rock, a river and royal stones

items.text: Dumbarton Rock was a formidable stronghold, but in 870 the Viking rulers Olaf and Ivar of Dublin besieged it for four months. The attackers took treasure and captives. The Irish Sea connected competing courts and also exposed communities to raiding and enslavement.

At Govan, ninth- to eleventh-century sculptured stones include crosses, grave slabs, five hogback monuments and an elaborate stone coffin. The concentration suggests royal patronage and burial. Archaeologists think political importance shifted upriver after Dumbarton’s defeat, rather than the British kingdom simply vanishing.

Near Govan church once stood the huge earthen Doomster Hill, interpreted as an assembly and justice site. It was demolished in the nineteenth century. Modern researchers use three-dimensional imaging of the surviving stones to recover worn carving and investigate how carvers worked.

sections.title: Welsh courts needed more than a throne

items.text: The thirteenth-century princes of Gwynedd used a network of courts. Excavation at Llys Rhosyr on Anglesey in 1992-1996 revealed remains later used to design the museum reconstruction at St Fagans. The reconstructed hall is a modern interpretation of archaeological evidence, not a surviving medieval palace.

Gwynedd’s 22 recorded courts included halls, kitchens, stables, barns, kennels and a privy, or toilet. Governing meant feeding people, storing supplies, caring for horses and handling waste. Even a prince needed somewhere to go when the meeting ran long.

Welsh law books attributed their tradition to Hywel Dda, who died in 950, but the earliest surviving copies are thirteenth-century. Peniarth MS 28 is a Latin copy made around that century’s middle. Its laws combine older material with later rules, so the manuscript is not Hywel’s own handbook.

Peniarth 28 pictures hair-pulling as an insult or injury requiring compensation and introduces rules concerning women with a woman holding a dish. Its animal pictures include a cat whose green pigment ate through the parchment. This particular cat has become a cat-shaped hole.

sections.title: Ireland: farms, towns and powerful households

items.text: Brian Boru became Ireland’s high-king but faced powerful opponents. At Clontarf in 1014 he died during his side’s victory over Irish and Scandinavian enemies. Historians debate the balance between a rebellion against his supremacy and a wider conflict; a simple Irish-versus-Viking story misses important alliances.

Cattle were a major measure of wealth in early medieval Ireland. From the eighth century, cereal farming became increasingly important: watermills and improved grain-drying kilns helped process surplus harvests. Political power rested partly on very practical questions about livestock, grain and who controlled their production.

Ballinderry crannog in County Westmeath was probably a wealthy Irish household’s island home. Its late ninth- to early eleventh-century finds include spinning, weaving and sewing tools, leather goods and wooden utensils. A decorated gaming board was probably used for hnefatafl, a game associated with the Viking world.

Later medieval Irish finds, overlapping this map’s closing decades and continuing beyond them, include wooden churns used for butter-making, sickles for harvesting grain and quern stones for grinding flour. Preparing food required tools, time and skilled hands long before anyone sat down to eat.

Viking-age Dublin’s houses had woven wooden walls, probably sealed with mud or dung. Craftspeople made wooden bowls, cups, toys and board games as well as tools and furniture. Rural households and Norse-linked towns exchanged goods and influences; they were not sealed cultural compartments.

sections.title: Children, learning and a very focused cat

items.text: Medieval Irish fosterage could build lasting relationships between children and another household. Legal and literary evidence includes care beginning in infancy, sometimes with wet-nursing. Arrangements varied: it is misleading to say that every child left home at seven or that foster parents always had one social rank.

Irish legal writers even considered injuries suffered by children at play. The Old Irish tract Mellbretha distinguished stages of youth ending at seven, twelve and seventeen. Those categories show attention to changing responsibility, although legal rules cannot tell us exactly how every family managed a scraped knee.

Messe ocus Pangur Bán, “I and white Pangur,” opens an Old Irish poem dated about 800-850, preserved in the continental Codex Sancti Pauli. Modern Roman type presents a scholar’s comparison of study with cat-hunting.

In 1169 Anglo-Norman forces arrived in Ireland after an invitation from the displaced king of Leinster, Diarmait Mac Murchada. Conquest, settlement and new castles followed. This was a transformation of an already contested political landscape, not the replacement of one unified Celtic empire.

ending.text: There was no shared fall in 1279. Strathclyde became part of Scotland; English expansion transformed Ireland while Gaelic communities and institutions continued. In Wales, Llywelyn ap Gruffudd’s death in 1282 and the conquest ended Rhosyr’s princely role. These different transitions belong to different kingdoms, not the disappearance of their peoples.
